Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *koḱs- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *kóḱsos Proto-Indo-Iranian *káćšas Sanskrit कक्ष (kákṣa) Kashmiri کَژھ Inherited from Sanskrit कक्ष (kákṣa), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *káćšas (“armpit”), from Proto-Indo-European *kóḱsos, from *koḱs- (“joint”) + *-os.. According to Turner, borrowed from another Indo-Aryan language, since the usual -kṣ- > -ch- is not seen. Inherited from Sanskrit च॒क्र॒वा॒क (cakravāká). Compare Assamese চাকৈ-চকোৱা (sakoi-soküa), Bengali চকাচকি (cokacoki), Hindi चकवा (cakvā) and Nepali चखेवाचखेवी (cakhevācakhevī).

Hypercorrection of Classical Persian بطک (bat̤ak, “duck”), a wanderwort related to Arabic بَطَّة (baṭṭa), بَطّ (baṭṭ) (which itself is from Classical Persian بت (bat), perhaps with the diminutive suffix ـه (-a)), Old Armenian բադ (bad) and Sanskrit वर्तक (vartaka, “quail”), among others. Cognate with Punjabi ਬਤਕ (batak), ਬੱਤਖ਼ (battax) / بَطَّخ (bat̤t̤ax), Gujarati બતક (batak), Sindhi बदक (badaka) / Sindhi بَدَڪَ (badaka), Marathi बदक (badak), Konkani बदक (badak), Odia ବତକ (bataka), Hindustani (Hindi बत्तख़ (battax) / Urdu بَطَّخ (battax)), and perhaps in the Dravidian languages, Telugu బాతు (bātu), Kannada ಬಾತುಕೋಳಿ (bātukōḷi), Malayalam വാത്ത (vātta).

e: flat-topped plateaus, also called Karewas, which may be slightly higher than the floor of the Kashmir Valley (~1600m ASL) or as high as 3000m ASL, sloping gently towards the valley; generally consisting of clay, silt, sand, and gravel, these plateaus likely formed as lacustrine deposits during the Pleistocene.

e: Banihal, the name of a village and a pass located to the south of the Kashmir Valley in the Pir Panjal range.
etymology: Known in Kalhaṇa's Rājatarangiṇi (12th c.) as बाणशाला (bāṇaśālā), analyzable as a compound of Sanskrit बाण (bāṇa, “arrow”) + शाला (śālā, “place, hall”), or Kashmiri بان (bān, “arrow”) + ہال (hāl, “place, hall”).

e: Pir Panjal, the name of the mountain range to the south and west of the Kashmir Valley.
etymology: From Sanskrit पञ्चाल (pañcāla). Known in Kṣemendra's Samayamātṛkā (11th c.) as पञ्चालधारा (pañcāladhārā).

e: the name of a district in the northern part of the Kashmir Valley, officially known as Baramulla
etymology: From Sanskrit वराहमूल (varāhamūla), analyzable as वराह (varāha, “boar”) + मूल (mūla, “root”).

e: the town of the same name which forms the district headquarters of the aforementioned district
etymology: From Sanskrit वराहमूल (varāhamūla), analyzable as वराह (varāha, “boar”) + मूल (mūla, “root”).

e: the name of a locality near the town of Baramulla, where Xuanzang spent his first night in Kashmir.
etymology: From Sanskrit हुष्कपुर (huṣkapura), named after Huvishka, the 2nd century Kushan emperor who is supposed to have founded it. An intermediate form, he-sh-ka-ra, has been found incised on a large stone block, from the 8th century, near a stupa at Fathgarh.

e: Mt. Harmukh, located in the district of Ganderbal, towards the north-east of the Kashmir Valley; its peak elevation is about 5300m ASL, and it is revered by Kashmiri Pandits as the abode of Shiva.
etymology: From Sanskrit हरमुकुट (haramukuṭa, “Shiva's diadem”), but a superficial analysis of the Kashmiri name suggests a compound of ہَر (har, “Shiva”) and مۄکھ (mọkh, “face”), resulting in later Mahātmyas giving the name हरमुख (haramukha, “Shiva's face”).

e: the Kashmiri name of Kolahoi Peak, located in the district of Anantnag, towards the east of the Kashmir Valley; its peak elevation is about 5425m ASL, making it the highest peak of the Kashmir Division.

Pandrethan, the name of a locality to the south-east of Srinagar, possibly the site of the Śrīnagarī supposedly founded by Ashoka, with the name later transferred to the contiguous Pravarapura, the modern-day Srinagar.
the name of a village in the Pulwama district, towards the centre-southern region of the Kashmir Valley, officially known as Khrew.

Burzahom, the name of a site towards the north-east of Srinagar city, where remnants of a Neolithic and Megalithic culture contemporaneous with and outlasting the Mature Phase of the Indus Valley Civilization, including skeletal remains, have been found atop a plateau (وُڈٕر (vuḍụr))
etymology: Compound of بُرزٕ (burzụ, “birch”), from Sanskrit भूर्ज (bhūrja), and ـہوم (hōm), from Sanskrit आश्रम (āśrama, “asylum, retreat”).

e: Parihaspore, the name of a town that the 8th century king of Kashmir, Lalitaditya Muktapida, built as his capital, 22 km northwest of Srinagar, atop a plateau (see وُڈٕر (vuḍụr)).
etymology: From Sanskrit परिहासपुर (parihāsapura), analyzable as परिहास (parihāsa, “merriment”) + पुर (pura, “town”).
